facts.title: Named From Magnetic Confusion
facts.text: Manganese was first isolated in 1774 by Swedish chemist Johan Gottlieb Gahn, who reduced the mineral pyrolusite with charcoal. Its name traces back to 'magnesia nigra' (black magnesia), a term once muddled with the minerals that gave us both magnesium and the magnet, since these dark ores were long confused with one another.

facts.title: Four Brittle Crystal Forms
facts.text: Pure manganese is hard yet extremely brittle, so brittle that it cannot be machined or worked like ordinary metals. At room temperature it adopts a bizarre crystal structure called alpha-manganese with 58 atoms packed into a single unit cell, and it shifts through four different solid forms (alpha, beta, gamma, delta) as it is heated toward its melting point of about 1246 degrees Celsius.

facts.title: The Rainbow Of Oxidation States
facts.text: Manganese is a chemical chameleon that can exist in oxidation states from minus three all the way up to plus seven. Each state has a signature color in solution: the plus two ion is pale pink, plus six gives a deep green manganate, and plus seven yields the intense purple of permanganate, making manganese chemistry a vivid playground for the periodic table.

facts.title: Steel's Secret Ingredient
facts.text: More than 90 percent of all manganese produced goes into making steel, where it removes unwanted oxygen and sulfur and dramatically improves strength. Hadfield steel, invented by Robert Hadfield in 1882 with about 12 to 14 percent manganese, becomes harder the more it is hammered, which is why it is used for railway crossings, rock crushers, and prison bars.

facts.title: Purple Crystals That Clean Water
facts.text: Potassium permanganate, KMnO4, forms striking dark purple crystals and is a powerful oxidizing agent used worldwide to purify drinking water, treat skin infections, and remove iron and odors from well water. In the chemistry lab it serves as a self-indicating titration reagent, since it turns colorless the instant it is fully reduced, signaling the endpoint without any added dye.

facts.title: Essential For Every Breath You Take
facts.text: Manganese is a trace element vital to life, sitting at the heart of enzymes like manganese superoxide dismutase that protects your mitochondria from damaging free radicals. Most strikingly, the oxygen-evolving complex in plant photosynthesis uses a cluster of four manganese atoms to split water molecules, meaning nearly all the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere is released with manganese's help.

facts.title: Treasure Nodules On The Seabed
facts.text: Vast fields of potato-sized lumps called manganese nodules carpet parts of the deep ocean floor, especially the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the Pacific. These nodules grow agonizingly slowly, sometimes only a few millimeters every million years, yet collectively they hold billions of tons of manganese along with nickel, cobalt, and copper, making them a tempting and controversial mining target.

facts.title: Painted In The Ice Age
facts.text: Long before it was a metal, manganese was a pigment: prehistoric artists used black manganese dioxide to paint animals on cave walls at sites like Lascaux in France around 17,000 years ago. The same compound also colors glass, and historically glassmakers added it as 'glassmaker's soap' to cancel out the green tint caused by iron impurities.

facts.title: A Metal You Can See In Space
facts.text: Manganese is forged in the explosive deaths of massive stars and in thermonuclear supernovae, then scattered across the galaxy to become part of new worlds. Astronomers measure manganese abundances in distant stars to trace the chemical history of the Milky Way, and the element ranks among the dozen most abundant metals in Earth's crust at roughly 0.1 percent by mass.

facts.title: Too Much Causes Manganism
facts.text: Although the body needs only tiny amounts, chronic overexposure to manganese dust, common among miners and welders, can cause a serious neurological disorder called manganism with symptoms resembling Parkinson's disease. This happens because excess manganese accumulates in the basal ganglia of the brain, a sobering reminder that an element essential for life can become a hazard at high doses.
